'''''Vicia villosa''''', known as the '''hairy vetch''', '''fodder vetch''' or '''winter vetch''', is a plant native to some of [[Europe]] and [[western Asia]]. It is a [[legume]], grown as a [[forage]] crop, [[fodder]] crop, [[cover crop]], and [[green manure]]. Although non-native, it occurs in all US states and is considered invasive by some states,<ref name="USDA_Forest">{{cite web |url=https://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/hairy-vetch.pdf It is also found in most Canadian provinces.

Hairy vetch is very similar to [[tufted vetch]] (''Vicia cracca''), the most noticeable difference being that tufted vetch has a smooth stem.

Several [[subspecies]] are recognized:
* ''Vicia villosa'' ssp. ''ambigua'' <small>(Guss.) Kerguelen</small> (= ssp. ''elegantissima'', ssp. ''pseudocracca'')
* ''Vicia villosa'' ssp. ''eriocarpa'' <small>(Hausskn.) P.W.Ball</small>
* ''Vicia villosa'' ssp. ''microphylla'' <small>(d'Urv.) P.W.Ball</small>
* ''Vicia villosa'' ssp. ''varia'' <small>(Host) Corb.</small> (= ssp. ''dasycarpa'')
* ''Vicia villosa'' ssp. ''villosa''

The species ''[[Vicia hirsuta]]'' is also called hairy vetch.

==Cultivation==
Hairy vetch is widely used by organic growers in the United States as a winter cover crop and in [[no-till farming]], as it is both winter hardy and can fix as much as 200 lb/acre of atmospheric nitrogen.<ref>{{Cite news
| last = Philpott
| first = Tom
| title = One Weird Trick to Fix Farms Forever
| work = Mother Jones
| access-date = 2014-03-14
| date = 2013-09-09
| url = https://www.motherjones.com/environment/2013/09/cover-crops-no-till-david-brandt-farms
}}</ref>  Disadvantages of hairy vetch in production agriculture are related to the crop having a portion of hard seed and its tendency to shatter seed early in the season, leading to it remaining in the field as a weed later in the season.  This can be a particular problem in wheat production.

==Companion plant==

Organic gardeners often plant hairy vetch (a nitrogen-fixing legume) as a [[companion plant]] to tomatoes, as an alternative to rotating crops in small growing areas.  When it is time to plant tomatoes in the spring, the hairy vetch is cut to the ground and the tomato seedlings are planted in holes dug through the matted residue and stubble. The vetch vegetation provides both nitrogen and an instant mulch that preserves moisture and keeps weeds from sprouting.<ref>[http://www.organicgardening.com/feature/0,7518,s1-5-16-1561,00.html Organic Gardening Magazine] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080412062629/http://www.organicgardening.com/feature/0,7518,s1-5-16-1561,00.html |date=April 12, 2008 }}</ref>

==Alien or invasive species==

It is regulated in the state of Florida.<ref name="Florida">{{cite web|url=https://www.invasive.org/browse/subinfo.cfm?sub=6614#myModal |title=hairy vetch  |publisher=Invasive.org Center for Invasive Species and Ecosystem Health |access-date=10 September 2017}}</ref> Some sources consider it generally invasive in areas with suitable climate for it to out-compete native species, in a manner similar to how cow vetch, ''[[Vicia cracca]]'', is regarded.<ref name="MN_DNR">{{cite web |url=http://www.dnr.state.mn.us/invasives/terrestrialplants/herbaceous/ |title=Cow vetch and hairy vetch |publisher=Minnesota DNR Department of Natural Resources |access-date=10 September 2017 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> With both vetches, their agricultural usefulness is typically given precedence over concerns regarding potential ecological degradation.<ref name="CABI">{{cite journal|url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/56371
